about_release: Generated release 0 of the Tribes of Behavior atlas (ADR-0003 §10). Hand-authored before the database existed; import_atlas loads it as release 0, after which the database is the truth and export_atlas regenerates these files. Do not hand-edit after import.
about: The arenas a history can be told in. A geo is a stretch of the graph paper that people have moved around inside more easily than across its edges — a peninsula, a basin, a steppe, a sea. Geos overlap on purpose: Iberia sits inside the Mediterranean and the Atlantic world at once, and each tells a different true story about it. box is [west, south, east, north] in degrees; when west > east the box crosses the antimeridian. aka holds the names other peoples and other eras gave the place — these are the first competing descriptors. Reconciling: a bundle declares the geo it was told from; tribes keep one id across every geo they appear in, so when two geos' histories describe the same tribe, their colonies are merged and disagreements are kept side by side with their geo as attribution, never silently overwritten.

kinds.basin: a river system or lowland that drains together
kinds.plain: open lowland with few internal barriers
kinds.desert: dry country crossed, not settled, except at oases
kinds.island: one island or a tight group
kinds.coast: a strip held together by the sea in front of it
kinds.corridor: a passage between two other worlds
kinds.sea: a body of water that is itself an arena
kinds.ocean: an ocean world — joined by sail, then by wire
kinds.globe: the whole sphere — for what is told at world scale

geos.name: Iberian Peninsula
geos.why: A near-island behind the Pyrenees: entered from the sea and from Africa as often as from Europe.

geos.name: Gaul
geos.why: Open country between Atlantic, Mediterranean and Rhine; every road from Italy to Britain crosses it.

geos.name: Low Countries
geos.why: The Rhine–Meuse–Scheldt delta: reclaimed land, cities and ships. Where Spinoza's Iberian exiles landed.

geos.name: British Isles
geos.why: Two big islands and many small, reached from the continent in waves and later reaching everywhere.

geos.name: North Atlantic islands
geos.why: Settled late, by boat, from Norway and Ireland — a society that wrote down its own founding.

geos.name: Alpine arc
geos.why: A wall with passes: valleys keep tongues and creeds apart; passes join north to south.

geos.name: Italian Peninsula
geos.why: A long spine in the middle of the Mediterranean, with Sicily, Sardinia and Corsica beside it.

geos.name: Central Europe (Rhine–Elbe–Danube)
geos.why: The land between the Rhine and the Elbe and the upper Danube; a patchwork for most of its history.

geos.name: Carpathian Basin
geos.why: The steppe's western cul-de-sac: Huns, Avars and Magyars all rode here and stopped.

geos.name: North European Plain (Oder–Vistula)
geos.why: Flat country without natural borders — borders here have been drawn and redrawn by armies.

geos.name: Scandinavia & Fennoscandia
geos.why: Fjords, forest and a shared sea: Norse, Sámi and Finnic worlds side by side.

geos.name: East European Plain (Dnieper–Volga)
geos.why: River roads from the Baltic to the Black Sea and Caspian; forest above, steppe below.

geos.name: Volga–Ural
geos.why: Where Turkic, Finno-Ugric and Slavic worlds meet on the middle Volga; Islam's northern edge since 922.

geos.name: Pontic–Caspian Steppe
geos.why: Grassland from the Danube to the Urals; homeland, on one reading, of the Indo-European tongues.

geos.name: Caucasus
geos.why: So many valleys, so many languages — the densest tongue-map on Earth.

geos.name: Balkan Peninsula
geos.why: Mountains that break peoples into pockets; the hinge between Rome, Constantinople and the steppe.

geos.name: Aegean world
geos.why: A sea of islands that joins Greece to Anatolia instead of dividing them.

geos.name: Anatolia
geos.why: A plateau bridge between Europe and Asia, crossed by every army and every creed.

geos.name: Levant
geos.why: A thin coast between sea and desert where three continents' roads cross; the origin of the alphabet and of three monotheisms.

geos.name: Fertile Crescent
geos.why: The arc of rain-fed and river-fed land where farming, cities and writing began.

geos.name: Mesopotamia
geos.why: The Tigris–Euphrates floodplain: irrigation, the first cities, the first written law.

geos.name: Iranian Plateau
geos.why: A high basin ringed by mountains; the seat of empires that ruled from the Aegean to the Indus.

geos.name: Arabian Peninsula
geos.why: Desert ringed by trading coasts; the cradle of Arabic and of Islam.

geos.name: Egypt & the Lower Nile
geos.why: A river oasis 1,000 km long; the longest continuous civilisation on the paper.

geos.name: Maghreb
geos.why: Atlas mountains and coast between sea and Sahara — Iberia's mirror across the Strait.

names.name: Jazirat al-Maghrib (the Island of the West)

geos.name: Libya (Tripolitania & Cyrenaica)
geos.why: Two coastal pockets — one facing Carthage, one facing Greece — with the desert between them.

names.name: Libya (to the Greeks: all of Africa)

geos.name: Sahara
geos.why: Not a wall but a sea: crossed by camel caravans carrying salt, gold, books and creeds.

geos.name: Sahel & Sudanic belt
geos.why: The southern shore of the desert sea: the empires of Ghana, Mali, Songhai, Kanem and their scholars.

geos.name: Senegambia
geos.why: Two rivers that let the Sahel reach the Atlantic.

geos.name: Middle Niger
geos.why: An inland delta in the dry belt — the anchor of West Africa's great states and manuscripts.

geos.name: Guinea coast & forest
geos.why: Forest kingdoms — Asante, Oyo, Benin, Igbo country — and the Atlantic trade that reached them.

names.name: the Gold Coast, Slave Coast & Bight of Benin

geos.name: Lake Chad Basin
geos.why: A closed basin at the end of the central Saharan road.

geos.name: Nubia & the Middle Nile
geos.why: Egypt's southern twin: pharaohs of its own, then Christian kingdoms for a thousand years.

geos.name: Upper Nile & the Sudd
geos.why: A vast swamp that stopped the Nile's northern powers; cattle peoples and their own long history.

geos.name: Horn of Africa & Ethiopian Highlands
geos.why: A highland fortress with its own script and an early Christianity, facing Arabia across a narrow sea.

geos.name: Swahili coast
geos.why: Stone towns facing the monsoon: Africa's Indian Ocean shore.

geos.name: African Great Lakes
geos.why: Fertile lake country with dense kingdoms long before writing reached it.

geos.name: Congo Basin
geos.why: River highways through the forest; the route of the Bantu expansion.

geos.name: Kongo & Angola coast
geos.why: A Christian kingdom from 1491, and the largest single source of the Atlantic slave trade.

geos.name: Zambezi & Great Zimbabwe
geos.why: Gold country on the plateau that fed the Swahili coast.

geos.name: Southern Africa
geos.why: Khoe-San, Bantu-speaking and settler worlds sharing — and fighting over — one plateau.

geos.name: Madagascar
geos.why: Settled from Borneo across the whole Indian Ocean — an Austronesian tongue off the African coast.

geos.name: Macaronesia
geos.why: The Atlantic stepping stones: the Guanches' islands, then the laboratory for plantations.

geos.name: Kazakh Steppe
geos.why: The steppe's long middle: nomad confederations moving between Mongolia and Europe.

geos.name: Transoxiana & the oases
geos.why: Oasis cities on the Amu and Syr Darya — Samarkand, Bukhara, Merv — the Silk Roads' middle.

geos.name: Afghanistan & the Hindu Kush
geos.why: Passes between Iran, India and Central Asia — Buddhism went north through here; Islam came south.

geos.name: Tarim Basin
geos.why: A ring of oases around the Taklamakan; Tocharian, Khotanese, Sogdian, then Uyghur.

geos.name: Dzungaria & the Tian Shan
geos.why: The steppe gate between Mongolia and the west.

geos.name: Mongolian Plateau
geos.why: Homeland of the steppe empires — Xiongnu, Türks, Uyghurs, Mongols.

geos.name: Tibetan Plateau
geos.why: The highest inhabited plateau; its own empire, then its own Buddhism.

geos.name: West Siberian Plain
geos.why: The world's largest flat land, drained by the Ob; reached by Russian fur traders after 1580.

geos.name: Central & Eastern Siberia
geos.why: Endless taiga; reindeer peoples and river routes to the Pacific.

geos.name: Amur & Okhotsk
geos.why: Where Manchurian, Siberian and Pacific worlds meet.

geos.name: Arctic Eurasia
geos.why: Tundra peoples from the Sámi to the Chukchi, joined by the ice edge.

geos.name: Beringia
geos.why: The door between Asia and the Americas, walked through when it was land.

geos.name: Indus Valley
geos.why: The Harappan cities' river, and India's door to Iran and Central Asia.

geos.name: Gujarat & Kathiawar
geos.why: India's western ports — Lothal, Cambay, Surat — and the merchants who sailed from them to Africa and Arabia.

geos.name: Indo-Gangetic Plain
geos.why: The great farming plain of the north: the Vedas, the Buddha, Mauryas, Mughals.

geos.name: Himalaya
geos.why: The wall between India and Tibet, with valley kingdoms in its folds.

geos.name: Bengal Delta
geos.why: The world's largest delta: rice, cloth, and a frontier where Islam spread by clearing forest.

geos.name: Deccan Plateau
geos.why: The high triangle of the peninsula, between the Ghats.

geos.name: Kalinga (Odisha)
geos.why: The east coast whose conquest turned Ashoka toward Buddhism; a launch point for voyages to Southeast Asia.

geos.name: Southern India
geos.why: Dravidian tongues and temple states facing two seas.

geos.name: Sri Lanka
geos.why: An island where Theravada Buddhism was kept and written down.

geos.name: Yellow River & North China Plain
geos.why: The loess and floodplain where Chinese writing and states began.

geos.name: Hexi Corridor
geos.why: A strip of oases that is China's only door west.

geos.name: Yangtze Basin
geos.why: Rice country that became the economic heart of China after 1000.

geos.name: Sichuan Basin
geos.why: A walled basin that keeps its own ways and grew rich on irrigation.

geos.name: Lingnan & the South China coast
geos.why: South of the mountains: a sea-facing China of ports and emigrants.

geos.name: Yunnan–Guizhou Plateau
geos.why: Highland kingdoms between China, Tibet and Southeast Asia.

geos.name: Manchuria
geos.why: Forest, steppe and farmland north of the Wall — the base of two conquest dynasties.

geos.name: Korean Peninsula
geos.why: A peninsula that took China's books and wrote its own alphabet.

geos.name: Japanese archipelago
geos.why: Islands close enough to borrow and far enough to choose.

geos.name: Ryukyu & Taiwan
geos.why: Island chain between China and Japan; Taiwan is where the Austronesian tongues began.

geos.name: Mainland Southeast Asia
geos.why: Parallel river valleys — Irrawaddy, Chao Phraya, Mekong, Red — each with its kingdom.

geos.name: Red River Delta
geos.why: A thousand years under China and a long history of turning that against it.

geos.name: Malay Peninsula
geos.why: The neck every ship between India and China had to pass — Melaka, then Singapore.

geos.name: Maritime Southeast Asia
geos.why: Islands joined by shallow seas: Srivijaya, Majapahit, and an Islam that came by trade.

geos.name: Philippine archipelago
geos.why: Seven thousand islands — and Spain's Pacific end of the world.

geos.name: Moluccas
geos.why: The only source of cloves and nutmeg — the prize the whole age of sail went looking for.

geos.name: New Guinea
geos.why: An independent invention of farming and a thousand languages on one island.

geos.name: Australia
geos.why: The longest-held continuous cultures on the paper, then a settler state after 1788.

geos.name: Aotearoa
geos.why: The last large land humans reached, by canoe, around 1280.

geos.name: Island Melanesia
geos.why: Where the Lapita voyagers first stepped off into the open Pacific.

names.name: the Solomons, Vanuatu, New Caledonia & Fiji

geos.name: Micronesia
geos.why: Atolls held together by star-path navigation.

geos.name: Polynesian Triangle
geos.why: The largest culture area on Earth, nearly all water, settled by navigators without instruments.

geos.name: Arctic North America & Greenland
geos.why: One Inuit world from Alaska to Greenland, and the Norse who failed to hold its edge.

geos.name: North American Subarctic
geos.why: Forest and lakes, canoe routes, and later the fur trade that drew the continent's map.

geos.name: Pacific Northwest coast
geos.why: Salmon-rich coast where foragers built ranked societies and great houses.

geos.name: California
geos.why: A pocket of extraordinary language diversity behind mountains and desert.

geos.name: American Southwest & Great Basin
geos.why: Pueblo farmers, Diné and Apache, and the northern reach of New Spain.

geos.name: Columbia Plateau & Northern Rockies
geos.why: Rivers and camas meadows between the Cascades and the Rockies; trade fairs at The Dalles drew the whole West.

geos.name: Northern Mexico
geos.why: The dry frontier between Mesoamerica and the Southwest — silver, missions and raiders.

geos.name: Great Plains
geos.why: Grassland that became a horse culture after the Spanish brought horses — an American steppe.

geos.name: Mississippi Valley & Eastern Woodlands
geos.why: Mound-building towns on the great river; the continent's interior highway.

geos.name: Great Lakes & St. Lawrence
geos.why: A freshwater sea and its river to the Atlantic — the route of the French and the fur trade.

geos.name: Atlantic seaboard & Appalachia
geos.why: Coastal plain behind a mountain wall; the beachhead of English settlement.

geos.name: Mesoamerica
geos.why: Maize, the calendar, writing and cities invented independently — Olmec to Mexica.

geos.name: Maya region
geos.why: City-states in the forest with the Americas' fullest writing system.

geos.name: Central American isthmus
geos.why: A land bridge between two continents and a crossing between two oceans.

geos.name: Caribbean
geos.why: Taíno and Kalinago islands, then the first and harshest laboratory of the Atlantic world.

geos.name: Northern Andes
geos.why: Three mountain chains with valleys between: Muisca goldwork and fierce regionalism.

geos.name: Orinoco & the Llanos
geos.why: Floodplain grassland — cattle country and a river road into the continent.

geos.name: Guiana Shield
geos.why: Ancient forest upland between the Orinoco and the Amazon; Maroon societies.

geos.name: Central Andes
geos.why: Civilisation built vertically — from coast desert to puna — Chavín, Moche, Tiwanaku, Inca.

geos.name: Southern Andes & Chile
geos.why: A strip between ocean and mountains; the Mapuche held it against the Inca and Spain.

geos.name: Amazonia
geos.why: A forest gardened by large societies that the record mostly forgot.

geos.name: Brazilian Highlands (Cerrado)
geos.why: Savanna upland — Jê peoples, then gold rushes and frontier.

geos.name: Atlantic coast of Brazil
geos.why: Tupi coast, then sugar, slavery and the largest African diaspora anywhere.

geos.name: Gran Chaco
geos.why: Hot dry plain that resisted conquest longest.

geos.name: Río de la Plata & the Pampas
geos.why: Grassland and estuary — gauchos, then the immigrants Europe shipped in.

geos.name: Patagonia & Tierra del Fuego
geos.why: Windswept steppe and channels at the far end of the human walk out of Africa.

geos.name: The Mediterranean
geos.why: Braudel's arena: one climate, one set of crops, three continents talking over water.

geos.name: Black Sea rim
geos.why: Greek colonies, steppe traders and Byzantium sharing one closed sea.

geos.name: Baltic rim
geos.why: Amber, Vikings, the Hanse — a northern Mediterranean.

geos.name: Red Sea corridor
geos.why: The narrow water joining the Mediterranean world to the Indian Ocean.

geos.name: Persian Gulf
geos.why: Mesopotamia's sea road to India since the Bronze Age.

geos.name: Silk Roads
geos.why: Not one road but a braid of routes from Chang'an to Antioch — goods moved short distances, ideas went the whole way.

geos.name: Indian Ocean world
geos.why: The first ocean crossed on a schedule: the monsoon blows one way half the year and back the other.

geos.name: Atlantic world
geos.why: Unused as a road until 1492, then the busiest one: conquest, plantation slavery, emigration, cable.

geos.name: Pacific world
geos.why: Crossed first by Polynesian canoes, then by the Manila galleon (1565), now by the cables that carry most of the world's data.

geos.name: Antarctica & the subantarctic
geos.why: The control case: a continent with no human history until 1820, governed by a treaty instead of a people.

names.name: Kerguelen, South Georgia & the Southern Ocean islands

geos.name: The whole globe
geos.why: For what spreads at the scale of the planet — printing, radio, the internet — and is better told once than 113 times.
